items.prompt: What is a "full table scan"?
choices: Checking every row in a table one by one until a match is found
A specialized index structure built just for fast full-text search
A complete copy of the database kept on a separate disk
A query that stops once it reads the very first matching row found
items.explanation: A full table scan checks every single row in order, looking for a match — its cost grows in direct proportion to the number of rows in the table.
items.reference:
🔎 Full scan — check row 1, row 2, row 3 ... until a match or the end
📈 Cost — grows linearly: 2x rows ≈ 2x checks

Why: without an index, this is the only way a database can find a row — nothing tells it where to look.

items.prompt: How does a full table scan's cost change as row count grows?
choices: It stays constant regardless of row count
It grows in direct (linear) proportion to row count
It shrinks as row count grows
It grows only if the table has an index
items.explanation: A full scan checks every row, so doubling the row count roughly doubles the number of checks needed — cost grows linearly with data size.
items.reference:
🔎 Full scan — check row 1, row 2, row 3 ... until a match or the end
📈 Cost — grows linearly: 2x rows ≈ 2x checks

Why: without an index, this is the only way a database can find a row — nothing tells it where to look.

items.prompt: What is a database index?
choices: A separate structure built ahead of time to make lookups on a column fast without scanning every row
A detailed log file recording, in order, every single query the database has ever executed
A complete backup copy of the table, kept automatically on a totally separate physical disk
A configuration setting that makes every single write to a table complete noticeably faster
items.explanation: An index is a separate, pre-built structure (sorted or hashed) mapping column values to row locations, so a lookup can jump close to the answer instead of scanning every row.
items.reference:
📖 Index — a dictionary's alphabetical order, not the book's chapter order
⚖️ Trade-off — costs disk space + slower writes, buys faster reads

Why: a dictionary lets you find a word without reading the whole book because its entries are pre-sorted — an index makes the same trade for a database column.

items.prompt: Which trade-off does adding a database index actually make?
choices: It's pure upside — meaningfully faster reads across the board, with no downside whatsoever
It uses extra disk space and slows down writes to the indexed column, in exchange for faster reads
It makes reads measurably slower while making writes to that same column faster instead
It only changes how the table's columns are displayed, never the actual query speed at all
items.explanation: An index needs its own storage, and every insert/update/delete on the indexed column has to update the index too — indexing trades write cost and disk space for read speed, not a free upgrade.
items.reference:
📖 Index — a dictionary's alphabetical order, not the book's chapter order
⚖️ Trade-off — costs disk space + slower writes, buys faster reads

Why: a dictionary lets you find a word without reading the whole book because its entries are pre-sorted — an index makes the same trade for a database column.

items.prompt: What makes a B-tree index different from a full table scan?
choices: It deliberately stores rows in a random, unsorted order purely to speed up write operations
It's a balanced, sorted tree structure where lookup cost grows logarithmically, not linearly, with row count
It only ever works correctly on numeric columns, and never on strings, dates, or booleans
It completely removes the need to store the original table's underlying row data at all
items.explanation: A B-tree keeps values sorted in a balanced tree, so a lookup only needs to make a handful of comparisons (roughly log2 of the row count) instead of checking every row.
items.reference:
🌳 B-tree — balanced, sorted tree
📉 Cost — O(log n): doubling rows adds ~1 comparison, not double the comparisons

Why: because the tree stays sorted, it also answers range queries ("age > 30") for free — a full scan or hash index can't say the same.

items.prompt: Roughly how does a B-tree's lookup cost grow as the row count grows?
choices: Logarithmically — doubling the rows adds only about one more comparison
Linearly — doubling the rows always doubles the comparisons needed
Exponentially — doubling the rows squares the comparisons required
It doesn't grow at all, no matter how many rows are added
items.explanation: A B-tree lookup cost is O(log n) — at 2,000,000 rows it takes roughly 21 comparisons, barely more than the ~9 comparisons needed at 500 rows.
items.reference:
🌳 B-tree — balanced, sorted tree
📉 Cost — O(log n): doubling rows adds ~1 comparison, not double the comparisons

Why: because the tree stays sorted, it also answers range queries ("age > 30") for free — a full scan or hash index can't say the same.

items.prompt: What is a hash index best suited for?
choices: Range queries, like finding every row whose value falls between two given bounds
Exact-match lookups, where average-case cost is constant regardless of row count
Sorting an entire table in place by the value of the indexed column
Finding the single row whose value is closest to a given target value
items.explanation: A hash index gives average O(1) exact-match lookups — but hashing destroys value order, so it can't answer range or sorted-output queries at all.
items.reference:
#️⃣ Hash index — O(1) average for exact match
🚫 Can't do — ranges, sorted output (order is scrambled)

Why: the same scrambling that makes lookups fast is what destroys the ordering a range query needs.

items.prompt: Why can't a hash index answer a range query like "find every row with age between 30 and 40"?
choices: Because hash indexes are inherently and unconditionally slower than B-trees for literally every kind of query imaginable
Because hashing scatters values into unrelated positions, so there's no way to know which values fall between two others without checking every one
Because range queries simply aren't a valid, well-formed kind of query that the SQL language supports at all
Because hash indexes are structurally only ever able to work correctly on string-typed columns, never on numbers
items.explanation: A hash function deliberately scrambles similar inputs into unrelated bucket positions — that's what makes lookups fast, but it also destroys the ordering a range query depends on.
items.reference:
#️⃣ Hash index — O(1) average for exact match
🚫 Can't do — ranges, sorted output (order is scrambled)

Why: the same scrambling that makes lookups fast is what destroys the ordering a range query needs.

items.prompt: What does "selectivity" mean for an indexed column?
choices: How much extra disk space the index's internal structure ends up taking up on disk over time
How much the index actually narrows a search — a mostly-unique column is highly selective, a mostly-repeated column is not
Whether or not the column is even allowed to contain NULL values in the first place
How frequently the values stored in that particular column happen to get updated over time
items.explanation: Selectivity measures how much an index narrows the search. A near-unique column like email narrows a lot; a column like a boolean flag with only two values narrows almost nothing.
items.reference:
🎯 High selectivity — email (mostly unique) narrows a lot
🪨 Low selectivity — is_active (2 values) narrows almost nothing

Why: an index only helps if following it actually eliminates most of the table — a low-selectivity index may not be worth using at all.

items.prompt: Why does an index on a boolean column like is_active (true/false) usually help a query very little?
choices: Because boolean columns simply can't be indexed by the database engine at all, under any configuration
Because with only two possible values, the index barely narrows the search — roughly half the table still matches either value
Because boolean indexes always take noticeably longer to build than any other kind of index
Because booleans are actually stored internally as plain text, which breaks indexing entirely
items.explanation: A column with only a couple of distinct values has low selectivity — an index on it still leaves a huge fraction of the table matching, so the database may reasonably prefer a full scan.
items.reference:
🎯 High selectivity — email (mostly unique) narrows a lot
🪨 Low selectivity — is_active (2 values) narrows almost nothing

Why: an index only helps if following it actually eliminates most of the table — a low-selectivity index may not be worth using at all.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, the login query took 2ms at 500 users and 400ms at 2,000,000 users. What changed about the query itself between those two points?
choices: The query itself was quietly rewritten to be less efficient
Nothing about the query changed — only the row count grew
The database engine running underneath it was downgraded
The email column used in the lookup was renamed along the way
items.explanation: The query and code were unchanged — the slowdown came entirely from the table outgrowing the point where a full scan was cheap enough to go unnoticed.
items.reference:
🐣 500 users — 2ms
📈 2,000,000 users — 400ms, same query

Why: an unindexed lookup's cost is tied to table size, not query complexity — growth alone is enough to make a fine query slow.

items.prompt: What is the most direct fix for the login query slowdown described in the opening scenario, without changing the query text?
choices: Add an index on the email column
Rewrite the query in a different programming language
Delete old user records to shrink the table
Increase the server's screen resolution
items.explanation: Adding an index on email lets the database jump close to the matching row instead of scanning all 2,000,000 rows — the query text doesn't need to change at all.
items.reference:
🐣 500 users — 2ms
📈 2,000,000 users — 400ms, same query

Why: an unindexed lookup's cost is tied to table size, not query complexity — growth alone is enough to make a fine query slow.

items.prompt: How is a database index similar to a dictionary?
choices: Both store their entries in precisely the order they were each originally entered, unsorted
Both are organized (sorted) specifically to let you find an entry without reading everything before it
Both require memorizing every single entry in the book ahead of time, cover to cover, by heart
Neither one actually has anything meaningful in common with the other at all, really
items.explanation: A dictionary's alphabetical order exists precisely so you can find a word without reading the whole book — an index makes the same trade for a database column.
items.reference:
📖 Index — a dictionary's alphabetical order, not the book's chapter order
⚖️ Trade-off — costs disk space + slower writes, buys faster reads

Why: a dictionary lets you find a word without reading the whole book because its entries are pre-sorted — an index makes the same trade for a database column.

items.prompt: Going from 500 to 2,000,000 rows is a 4,000x increase in data. Roughly how many more comparisons does a B-tree lookup need at 2,000,000 rows compared to 500?
choices: About 4,000x more comparisons, precisely matching the increase in rows
About 12 more comparisons total (21 vs. 9) — barely more, not proportionally more
Exactly the same number of comparisons, with zero increase whatsoever at all
About 100x more comparisons, far below the full 4,000x row increase
items.explanation: A B-tree's cost is O(log n) — log2(2,000,000) ≈ 21 vs. log2(500) ≈ 9, so a 4,000x growth in data adds only about 12 more comparisons, not a proportional increase.
items.reference:
📊 Full scan — 500 → 2,000,000 checks (linear)
🌳 B-tree — 9 → 21 comparisons (logarithmic)

Why: linear vs. logarithmic is the whole story — the same 4,000x data growth means 4,000x more full-scan work but barely any more B-tree work.

items.prompt: What is the key difference between how full-scan cost and B-tree lookup cost grow as row count increases?
choices: Full scan grows linearly with row count; B-tree grows logarithmically
Both grow at exactly the same rate as the row count increases
Full scan grows logarithmically; B-tree grows linearly instead
Neither one grows at all as the row count keeps increasing
items.explanation: Full scan cost is O(n) — directly proportional to row count. B-tree lookup cost is O(log n) — it barely grows even as row count grows enormously.
items.reference:
📊 Full scan — 500 → 2,000,000 checks (linear)
🌳 B-tree — 9 → 21 comparisons (logarithmic)

Why: linear vs. logarithmic is the whole story — the same 4,000x data growth means 4,000x more full-scan work but barely any more B-tree work.

items.prompt: Which of these can a B-tree index do that a hash index cannot?
choices: Perform a simple exact-match lookup on the indexed column, nothing more
Answer a range query like WHERE age > 30, or return results in sorted order
Store more than one column at once inside a single composite index
Be used at all by a relational database's query planner and engine
items.explanation: Because a B-tree keeps values in sorted order, it can answer range queries and sorted output for free. A hash index's scrambled bucket layout can't support either.
items.reference:
B-treeHash
Exact matchO(log n)O(1) avg
Range query✅ yes❌ no
Sorted output✅ free❌ no

Why: the hash function's scrambling is what makes lookups O(1) — it's the same mechanism that destroys the order a range query needs.

items.prompt: For a typical exact-match-only lookup (like a session-token cache keyed by an opaque token that's never sorted or range-queried), which index type is usually the better fit?
choices: A hash index — no ranges or sorting will ever be needed, so its O(1) average lookup is pure upside
A B-tree — it's always strictly the better overall choice over a hash index, in every case
Neither type — indexes should never be used for simple cache-like lookups at all, ever
It genuinely doesn't matter at all; both perform identically in every single situation
items.explanation: When range queries and sorted output will genuinely never be needed, a hash index's O(1) average exact-match lookup is the better fit — the B-tree's extra range capability isn't being used, so its slightly higher per-lookup cost buys nothing here.
items.reference:
B-treeHash
Exact matchO(log n)O(1) avg
Range query✅ yes❌ no
Sorted output✅ free❌ no

Why: the hash function's scrambling is what makes lookups O(1) — it's the same mechanism that destroys the order a range query needs.

items.prompt: Why does WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com' typically fail to use an index on email, while WHERE email LIKE 'alice%' can use it?
choices: A leading wildcard means a match could start anywhere in the string, so sorted order can't narrow the search — a trailing wildcard still lets sorted order narrow from the front
LIKE queries can never use an index at all, regardless of wildcard position, because pattern matching always requires reading every single row in the table
The '%' character is actually invalid SQL syntax in both positions, so these queries would fail with a parse error before ever running
Trailing wildcards are always slower to evaluate than leading wildcards, no matter how the underlying index structure happens to be built
items.explanation: A leading wildcard ('%...') means the match could start anywhere, so the sorted order an index relies on doesn't help. A trailing wildcard ('alice%') still lets the index narrow the search to entries starting with 'alice'.
items.reference:
❌ LIKE '%@x.com' — match could start anywhere, index can't help
✅ LIKE 'alice%' — sorted order narrows from the front
❌ WHERE LOWER(email)=? — indexes the raw value, not the function's output

Why: an index only helps when its sort order actually narrows the search — these patterns each break that in a different way.

items.prompt: A query uses WHERE LOWER(email) = 'alice@example.com' on a table with a plain index on email. Why might this query not use that index?
choices: Because the index was built on the raw email values, not on the output of LOWER(email) — the database would need a separate index on the expression itself
Because LOWER() is not considered a valid SQL function in most relational database systems, so this query would simply fail outright
Because indexes are only ever structurally able to work on numeric columns, never on text columns like email at all
Because equality comparisons like this one never make use of an index at all, regardless of the column's actual declared type
items.explanation: An index on email matches raw stored values. Applying a function like LOWER() changes what's being looked up, so the plain index doesn't match unless an index on the expression itself was created.
items.reference:
❌ LIKE '%@x.com' — match could start anywhere, index can't help
✅ LIKE 'alice%' — sorted order narrows from the front
❌ WHERE LOWER(email)=? — indexes the raw value, not the function's output

Why: an index only helps when its sort order actually narrows the search — these patterns each break that in a different way.

items.prompt: Why isn't "just add an index to every column" a good default strategy?
choices: Because most relational databases only ever support a hard maximum of two indexes per table, total
Because every index costs disk space and slows down writes to that column, whether or not it ever gets used by a query
Because adding an index to a column actually makes read queries slower instead of faster, always
Because indexes are automatically deleted by the database engine after exactly 30 days of disuse
items.explanation: Each index is extra storage and has to be updated on every write to that column — indexing a column nobody queries that way trades write performance for a read benefit that's never used.
items.reference:
💾 Every index — costs disk space
🐢 Every write — must update every index on that column
🎯 Right call — match indexes to actual query patterns, not "just in case"

Why: an index only pays for itself if the read savings outweigh the ongoing write cost — that's not automatic.

items.prompt: A table has an index on last_name, but every query filters by last_name AND birth_year together. What's the issue?
choices: There's genuinely no issue at all here — the existing last_name index already fully optimizes this exact combined query on its own
The index on last_name alone doesn't match the actual query pattern — a combined index on (last_name, birth_year) would serve this specific query better
Indexes can only ever be built against a single column at a time, so a query like this one can never be optimized
birth_year should categorically never be referenced inside any WHERE clause, under any circumstances whatsoever
items.explanation: An index should generally match how columns are actually queried together. An index on last_name alone still leaves birth_year filtering unindexed for this query — a composite index on both matches the real access pattern.
items.reference:
💾 Every index — costs disk space
🐢 Every write — must update every index on that column
🎯 Right call — match indexes to actual query patterns, not "just in case"

Why: an index only pays for itself if the read savings outweigh the ongoing write cost — that's not automatic.

items.prompt: L2 shows two separate charts (full scan vs. B-tree) instead of one combined chart. Why?
choices: Because Mermaid is technically and categorically incapable of ever rendering two separate data series within a single chart
Because putting both on one linear axis would flatten the B-tree's tiny bars to invisible slivers next to the full scan's much larger numbers
Because the two charts actually represent completely unrelated sets of data with no shared meaning between them at all
Because the full-scan data and the B-tree data were each measured using different, incompatible row counts entirely

📈 Chart 2 — B-tree, y-axis 0–25
🔗 Shared — same 5 row counts on both x-axes

items.prompt: Looking at L2's two charts, what does the B-tree chart's near-flat shape across 500 to 2,000,000 rows actually demonstrate?
choices: That the B-tree index implementation actually stops functioning correctly once row counts get sufficiently high
That B-tree lookup cost grows so slowly (logarithmically) that a 4,000x increase in rows is barely visible in comparison cost
That the chart rendering itself simply contains a visual error or rendering glitch of some unexplained kind
That B-tree indexes are only ever designed to function correctly up to exactly 2,000,000 total rows and no further

items.prompt: Implement `binarySearchByEmail(sortedUsers, email)`. `sortedUsers` is an array of `{ id, email }` objects already sorted ascending by `email`. Return the matching user object, or `null` if no row has that exact email. Use binary search — don't scan the array linearly.

tests.description: finds a row present at a known position
tests.expr: (() => { const users = Array.from({length: 500}, (_, i) => ({ id: i, email: `user${String(i).padStart(7,'0')}@example.com` })); const r = binarySearchByEmail(users, 'user0000250@example.com'); return expect(r && r.id).toBe(250); })()

tests.description: returns null for an email that isn't in the data
tests.expr: (() => { const users = Array.from({length: 500}, (_, i) => ({ id: i, email: `user${String(i).padStart(7,'0')}@example.com` })); return expect(binarySearchByEmail(users, 'nope@example.com')).toBe(null); })()

tests.description: finds the first row in the sorted array
tests.expr: (() => { const users = Array.from({length: 500}, (_, i) => ({ id: i, email: `user${String(i).padStart(7,'0')}@example.com` })); const r = binarySearchByEmail(users, 'user0000000@example.com'); return expect(r && r.id).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: finds the last row in the sorted array
tests.expr: (() => { const users = Array.from({length: 500}, (_, i) => ({ id: i, email: `user${String(i).padStart(7,'0')}@example.com` })); const r = binarySearchByEmail(users, 'user0000499@example.com'); return expect(r && r.id).toBe(499); })()

items.explanation: Binary search halves the remaining range on each comparison by checking the midpoint and discarding the half that can't contain the target. Because sortedUsers is ordered by email, this reaches any row in O(log n) comparisons instead of scanning every row — this is the same lookup behavior a real B-tree provides, without the on-disk tree machinery.
items.reference:
🌳 B-tree behavior — sorted array + binary search
📉 Cost — O(log n), ~9 comparisons at 500 rows, ~21 at 2,000,000

Why: this is L3's exact `binarySearchByEmail` function — the same one benchmarked against a full scan.

items.prompt: Implement `rangeQuerySorted(sortedUsers, fromEmail, toEmail)`. `sortedUsers` is sorted ascending by `email`. Return an array of every user whose `email` is between `fromEmail` and `toEmail`, inclusive on both ends, in ascending order. Use binary search to find the starting point rather than scanning from the beginning.

tests.description: returns exactly the 5 rows in a known range
tests.expr: (() => { const users = Array.from({length: 500}, (_, i) => ({ id: i, email: `user${String(i).padStart(7,'0')}@example.com` })); const r = rangeQuerySorted(users, 'user0000100@example.com', 'user0000104@example.com'); return expect(r.map(u => u.id)).toEqual([100,101,102,103,104]); })()

tests.description: returns an empty array when nothing matches
tests.expr: (() => { const users = Array.from({length: 500}, (_, i) => ({ id: i, email: `user${String(i).padStart(7,'0')}@example.com` })); const r = rangeQuerySorted(users, 'zzz1@example.com', 'zzz2@example.com'); return expect(r.length).toBe(0); })()

(() => { const users = Array.from({length: 500}, (_, i) => ({ id: i, email: `user${String(i).padStart(7,'0')}@example.com` })); const r = rangeQuerySorted(users, 'user0000010@example.com', 'user0000010@example.com'); return expect(r.map(u => u.id)).toEqual([10]); })()

items.explanation: Binary search locates the first row whose email is >= fromEmail, then a simple forward walk collects rows until email exceeds toEmail. Because the data is sorted, this only touches rows actually in range — a hash index has no equivalent operation, since hashing destroys the ordering this relies on.
items.reference:
🔍 Step 1 — binary search for the range's start
➡️ Step 2 — walk forward until past the range's end
🚫 A hash index can't do this — order is scrambled at build time

Why: this is exactly why B-tree indexes remain the default choice even though hash indexes can be faster for pure exact-match lookups.

items.prompt: L3's benchmark shows the full scan slowed down about 6,200x while the binary search only slowed down about 7x, when going from 500 to 2,000,000 rows (a 4,000x increase in data). What does this demonstrate?
choices: That binary search is fundamentally and rather unexpectedly broken once row counts get sufficiently large for any real workload
That linear-cost operations (full scan) degrade roughly proportional to data growth, while logarithmic-cost operations (binary search / B-tree) barely degrade at all
That the benchmark's underlying measurements are simply unreliable and shouldn't be trusted at all, in general, by anyone
That 2,000,000 rows is just categorically too many for any real production database to ever realistically handle correctly
items.explanation: This is the practical, measured version of the O(n) vs. O(log n) difference: a 4,000x data increase means roughly 4,000x more full-scan work (plus real hardware effects like cache misses push it even higher), but the binary search barely notices.
items.reference:
RowsFull scanBinary search
5000.0022ms0.00017ms
2,000,00013.47ms0.0012ms

Why: these are L3's actual measured numbers, not estimates — the gap is the same linear-vs-logarithmic story, now with real timings attached.

items.prompt: L3 notes that the full scan's real slowdown (~6,200x) was higher than the row-count increase (4,000x). What's the most likely explanation given the unit's own framing?

items.prompt: A table has an index on a low-selectivity column. Will the database's query planner always use that index when the column appears in a WHERE clause?
choices: Yes — if an index exists on a given column, the query planner is always strictly required to use it
Not necessarily — the planner may estimate a full scan is cheaper than following an index into a very large fraction of matching rows
No — indexes are only ever consulted for ORDER BY clauses, and are never used at all for WHERE filtering
It depends solely and entirely on the table's total row count, and never on the column's own selectivity
items.explanation: Having an index doesn't force its use. A query planner estimates cost, and following a low-selectivity index into millions of matching rows can genuinely be more expensive than just scanning — so the planner may reasonably skip the index.
items.reference:
🧮 Planner — estimates cost, doesn't blindly use every index
🪨 Low selectivity — following the index may cost more than scanning

Why: an index existing and an index being used are two different things — the planner decides based on estimated cost.

items.prompt: Why might a database's query planner choose a full scan over an existing index for a particular query?

Because indexes automatically expire and stop being usable after some fixed number of queries have run against them already
Because full table scans are technically and explicitly mandated by the SQL language's own formal syntax rules, without exception
items.explanation: The planner picks whichever strategy it estimates is cheaper for that specific query — an index isn't automatically the winner, especially against a low-selectivity column where it barely narrows the search.
items.reference:

🪨 Low selectivity — following the index may cost more than scanning

Why: an index existing and an index being used are two different things — the planner decides based on estimated cost.

items.prompt: What is a composite (multi-column) index best suited for?
choices: Queries that filter or sort on more than one of the indexed columns together, matching the actual combined access pattern
Making every single-column query against the table automatically and uniformly faster, with no other changes needed
Replacing the underlying table's need to have its own dedicated primary key entirely, once it exists
Storing several redundant copies of the exact same table purely for safety and disaster recovery reasons
items.explanation: A composite index is built to match a query pattern that filters on multiple columns together — e.g. (last_name, birth_year) — something a single-column index on either alone doesn't fully serve.
items.reference:
🧩 Composite index — one index over multiple columns, e.g. (last_name, birth_year)
🎯 Fits — queries that filter on that exact column combination

Why: the right index matches the actual query pattern, not just "this column looks important on its own."

items.prompt: A table has separate single-column indexes on last_name and on birth_year. Every query filters WHERE last_name = ? AND birth_year = ? together. What would likely serve this query pattern better?
choices: A single composite index on (last_name, birth_year) built specifically for that combined lookup
Deleting both of the existing single-column indexes outright, since neither one is genuinely useful
Adding a third, completely unrelated index on the email column instead of fixing the real problem
Nothing at all — two single-column indexes are always functionally equivalent to one composite index
items.explanation: Two separate single-column indexes don't combine into the same thing as one composite index built for the exact (last_name, birth_year) pattern the queries actually use — the composite index is purpose-built for this access pattern.
items.reference:

Why: the right index matches the actual query pattern, not just "this column looks important on its own."

items.prompt: L3 asks you to try writing a range query against `buildHashIndex`'s `Map`. What's the fundamental problem?
choices: JavaScript's built-in Map object doesn't actually expose any kind of working .get() method at all, by design
There's no way to ask a Map for "every key between X and Y" without iterating every entry — the same full-scan cost the index was supposed to eliminate
Map objects are structurally only able to hold string keys, not the structured email values used in this example here
Map objects turn out to be measurably slower than plain JavaScript objects for absolutely every single operation performed
items.explanation: A Map's keys are scattered across hash buckets with no relationship to their sorted order — answering a range query requires checking every entry, which reintroduces the exact O(n) cost an index exists to avoid.
items.reference:
#️⃣ Map.get(key) — O(1), exact match only
🚫 Map + range — no operation for "keys between X and Y"; only full iteration

Why: this is the concrete, code-level version of "hashing destroys order" — there's no shortcut, only iterate-and-check.

items.prompt: Why does iterating every entry of a hash-based Map to answer a range query defeat the entire purpose of having an index?
choices: It doesn't actually defeat the purpose at all — iterating a Map is exactly as fast as a binary search would be
Because checking every entry one by one is exactly the O(n) full-scan cost the index existed to eliminate in the first place
Because Map objects don't actually support any form of iteration over their own entries at all, by design
Because range queries turn out to be rare enough in practice that this extra cost basically never really matters
items.explanation: The entire point of an index is avoiding an O(n) check-every-row cost. Falling back to iterating every Map entry for a range query brings that exact cost right back — the hash index provides no advantage for this kind of query.
items.reference:
#️⃣ Map.get(key) — O(1), exact match only
🚫 Map + range — no operation for "keys between X and Y"; only full iteration

Why: this is the concrete, code-level version of "hashing destroys order" — there's no shortcut, only iterate-and-check.

items.prompt: L3's extend-it question asks about `WHERE email IN (id1, ..., id500)` — 500 exact-match lookups in one query — versus a single lookup. Does the hash index's per-lookup O(1) advantage over the B-tree's O(log n) matter more, less, or about the same at that batch size?
choices: It matters more overall, since the per-lookup gap is now paid 500 times instead of once, even though each individual gap is still small
It disappears completely — running the lookups as one batch somehow makes both index types exactly equal
It matters noticeably less, since batching somehow removes the actual need to look anything up at all, in any form
The comparison becomes entirely meaningless, since IN queries never make use of an index in the first place
items.explanation: Each lookup still costs roughly O(1) (hash) vs. O(log n) (B-tree) individually, so doing 500 of them multiplies whatever small per-lookup gap exists by 500 — the total absolute time difference grows, even though the *relationship* between the two costs per lookup hasn't changed.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Single lookup — gap is a fraction of a millisecond, easy to ignore
🔁 500 lookups — same per-lookup gap, now paid 500 times

Why: this is the same underlying cost difference as a single lookup — batching doesn't change the relationship, it just makes the total more visible.

items.prompt: If a hash index's per-lookup advantage over a B-tree is a fraction of a millisecond for one query, why would that advantage ever be worth choosing a hash index over a B-tree in practice?

Because B-trees apparently stop functioning correctly once the system comes under sufficiently heavy concurrent load for long enough
Because hash indexes somehow get progressively faster the more lookups are performed against them over time, without limit
